fixes.explanation: Assyria isn't named in this verse, baker. The text says Manasseh followed the abominations of the nations the LORD had driven out before the Israelites. That's the answer, right there in verse 2.

Not this time, friend, even though Hezekiah did the hard work of tearing them down. Verse 3 says Manasseh rebuilt the high places his father Hezekiah had destroyed. Somebody swept the whole floor and then the son dumped it all back out.
Altars it is, baker. Verse 3 says Manasseh raised up altars for Baal, a false god. He didn't just let the old places stand there. He raised up new altars for Baal.
Both, baker. Verse 5 says that in both courtyards of the house of the LORD, he built altars to all the host of heaven. Not one courtyard, but both. I think that's why the verse is so heavy.
Not quite, friend. The verse says that in both courtyards of the house of the LORD, Manasseh built altars to all the host of heaven. That's more than one courtyard. Both of them had altars.

Mediums, baker. Verse 6 says Manasseh practiced sorcery and divination, and consulted mediums and spiritists. The text calls it great evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking Him to anger. I'll stick to asking the LORD, and a good oven timer.

I have to say no to this one, baker. In verse 8 the LORD says, “…if only they are careful to do all I have commanded them…” and points to the Law that Moses, Israel's leader, commanded. Building altars isn't the condition. Doing what He commanded is.

It's actually the opposite, friend. In verse 12 the LORD, the God of Israel, says, “Behold, I am bringing such calamity upon Jerusalem and Judah…” Calamity, not peace and security. It's a hard word, and the LORD says it plainly.
Yes, baker. Verse 14 says God will forsake the remnant of His inheritance and deliver them into the hands of their enemies. It's a hard thing to read. I won't dress it up, because the text doesn't.

That's right, baker. Verse 18 says Manasseh rested with his fathers and was buried in his palace garden, the garden of Uzza. His son Amon reigned in his place. Verse 26 says Amon was buried in that garden too.
Not the temple courtyard, baker. Verse 18 says Manasseh was buried in his palace garden, the garden of Uzza. That's where the text puts him, so that's where I leave him.

True, baker. Verse 20 says Amon, Manasseh's son, did evil in the sight of the LORD, as his father Manasseh had done. Verse 21 says he walked in all the ways of his father. I wish it were different, friend.
The text says the opposite, friend. Verse 20 says Amon, Manasseh's son, did evil in the sight of the LORD, as his father Manasseh had done. Verse 21 adds that he walked in all the ways of his father.
Idols, baker. Verse 21 says Amon walked in all the ways of his father, and he served and worshiped the idols his father had served. Those were the same idols his father had served.
Yes, baker. Verse 23 says the servants of Amon conspired against him and killed the king in his palace. The text doesn't give a reason, so I won't make one up.
Babylon's king isn't in this scene, baker. Verse 23 says the servants of Amon conspired against him and killed the king in his palace. The plot came from his own servants.
